extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply principles from classical political economy (Adam Smith) to evaluate trade regulations such as import restraints, bounties, drawbacks, treaties, and colonial monopolies, focusing on their effects on a nation's real wealth, annual produce, and direction of industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth not identical to gold and silver
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular notion that wealth consists in money, or in gold and silver, is absurd; the annual produce of the land and labour of the country is the ultimate resource which constitutes real wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate national prosperity solely by bullion imports or stockpiles. Policies aimed only at increasing gold and silver (bullion) may not increase the real wealth or revenue of the society. Consider the value of annual produce and consumable goods instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary benefits of foreign trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign trade carries out the surplus part of the produce for which there is no domestic demand and brings back in return something else for which there is demand; it gives value to superfluities and opens wider markets that encourage division of labour and improvements of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess trade by whether it lets domestic producers realize value for their surplus, expands markets to allow greater specialization, and thereby increases the productive powers of labour and annual real revenue, not by bullion flows alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullion importation is a minor benefit of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Importing gold and silver is part of foreign commerce but a most insignificant part; a country carrying on foreign trade merely to import bullion would rarely need to freight a ship in a century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating bullion inflows as the principal measure of trade's success. Evaluate broader production, consumption, and market-expanding effects instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial system's six principal means to favour bullion balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial system proposes to increase the quantity of gold and silver by: (1) restraints upon importation of goods producible at home; (2) restraints upon importation of goods from particular disadvantageous countries; (3) drawbacks; (4) bounties; (5) advantageous treaties of commerce; (6) establishment of colonies/monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to categorize trade interventions. For each instrument, examine its actual effects on the annual produce, the direction of industry, and whether it genuinely augments national well‑being or merely redistributes profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on imports of goods producible at home
rubrics_metrics.description: By restraining (via high duties or prohibitions) the importation of foreign goods that can be produced domestically, the monopoly of the home market is secured to the domestic industry producing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate such restraints by: whether they merely grant local monopolies and divert capital into less advantageous employments; whether domestic production can match foreign price/quality; and their effect on the exchangeable value of the annual produce. If domestic production is costlier, the regulation is likely hurtful rather than beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on imports from particular countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraints (duties or prohibitions) imposed specifically on goods from countries with which the balance of trade is supposed disadvantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess targeted restraints for their actual impact on trade balances and domestic industry direction; beware of simplistic assumptions that blocking imports from certain countries will materially 'bring money in' or increase real national wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawbacks (rebates on duties upon export)
rubrics_metrics.description: When home manufactures are subject to duty or excise, the whole or part of it is frequently drawn back upon their exportation; likewise, duties paid on imported goods that are exported again are sometimes returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider drawbacks as mechanisms to avoid double taxation of goods crossing borders; evaluate whether they efficiently promote export without distorting production toward unprofitable industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties for encouraging particular industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties are given to encourage certain beginning manufactures or sorts of industry deemed to deserve special favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bounties cautiously: they may help initiate industries, but they can misdirect capital if the protected industry would not be competitive otherwise. Examine long‑term viability and opportunity cost of subsidizing particular sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous commercial treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: By procuring particular privileges in a foreign state for a country's goods and merchants beyond those granted to others, advantageous treaties are used to promote exports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate treaties for whether they genuinely open markets and increase returns to domestic producers, or simply redistribute trade gains. Also consider reciprocity and effects on domestic industry specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of colonies and monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing colonies in distant countries can procure particular privileges and often a monopoly for the goods and merchants of the founding country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess colonial/monopoly arrangements for whether exclusive access meaningfully increases national annual produce or simply concentrates profit. Examine long‑term costs, administrative burdens, and whether monopoly leads to inefficient allocation of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: General industry limited by capital; policy cannot increase it
rubrics_metrics.description: The general industry of a society cannot exceed what its capital can employ; regulations of commerce can only divert industry into different channels, not increase the aggregate industry beyond capital's capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge policies by whether they merely redirect existing capital (possibly harmfully) rather than increase productive capital. Favor measures that enable capital accumulation (savings) rather than artificial reallocation that reduces exchangeable value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private interest directs capital more effectively than state direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every individual, pursuing his own advantage, naturally directs capital into employments that are advantageous to the society; a statesman cannot safely or effectively direct private people's employment of capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer policies that allow individuals to choose investments (within reasonable rules) rather than prescriptive direction by the state. Be skeptical of regulations aiming to micromanage capital allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence of buying when foreign cheaper than domestic
rubrics_metrics.description: If a foreign country can supply a commodity cheaper than it can be made at home, it is prudent to buy it rather than produce it domestically; attempting to make at home what is cheaper to buy diminishes the exchangeable value of annual produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should not protect industries that are less efficient than foreign suppliers. Protection in such cases diverts industry from more advantageous employments and reduces national revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures (fine goods) are best exports to fund distant wars
rubrics_metrics.description: Finer and more improved manufactures, which contain great value in small bulk, are the commodities most proper to transport to distant countries to purchase pay and provisions for armies or to obtain money of the mercantile republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating wartime economic strategy, prioritize developing and exporting manufactured goods with high value‑to‑bulk ratios rather than bulky rudimentary agricultural produce. Recognize that transport of commodities often yields merchant profit, whereas sending bullion to pay debts yields none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rude produce unsuitable for supporting expensive/distant wars
rubrics_metrics.description: No foreign war of great expense or duration could conveniently be carried on by the exportation of the rude produce of the soil; sending large quantities would be too expensive and would deprive inhabitants of necessary subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For financing prolonged distant military engagements, do not rely on exporting bulky agricultural staples; evaluate the domestic subsistence cost and transport inefficiencies before promoting such exports.
